paragraphs.text: ReNU syndrome is an autosomal dominant syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder caused by de novo or inherited heterozygous variants in RNU4-2. RNU4-2 encodes the U4 snRNA of the major spliceosome U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP. Greene et al. (2024) described the syndrome as including intellectual disability, microcephaly, short stature, hypotonia, seizures and motor delay. Chen et al. (2024) found that the causative variants lie within an 18-bp region of RNU4-2 that maps to the T-loop and stem III of the U4/U6 duplex and is severely depleted of variation in the general population.

paragraphs.text: Chen et al. (2024) collected detailed phenotypes for 49 individuals (21 female and 28 male; median age 10 years, range 2 to 38). Of these, 42 had the n.64_65insT variant, 3 had other insertions, and 4 had single-nucleotide variants (SNVs). All had moderate to severe global developmental delay and intellectual disability. Most (83%) learned to walk, but late (mean age 3.4 years), and some had a wide-based or ataxic gait. Most were nonverbal. Other common features were short stature (76%), microcephaly (77%, mostly congenital), hypotonia (87%), seizures (77%; median age at onset 3 years), abnormal brain MRI (91%), vision problems (79%), autism (48%), feeding difficulties, and constipation. Of 48 individuals assessed, 45 had dysmorphic facial features. These varied, but included a myopathic face with deep-set eyes, epicanthus, a wide nasal bridge, anteverted nares or underdeveloped alae nasi, large cupped ears, full cheeks, full lips with downturned corners, a high-arched palate, and a large or protruding tongue. In most individuals brain MRI was abnormal, most often showing reduced white matter volume, hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, ventriculomegaly, and delayed myelination. Many organ systems were involved, including skeletal (osteopenia, recurrent fractures, scoliosis, kyphosis, hip dysplasia), endocrine (hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, pituitary abnormalities), visual (including cortical blindness), genitourinary, dental, and cutaneous systems. Presentation did not differ significantly between males and females.

paragraphs.text: Greene et al. (2024) ran a genetic association analysis on whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data from the UK 100,000 Genomes Project. They compared the burden of rare variants in 41,132 noncoding genes between 5,529 unrelated intellectual disability cases and 46,401 unrelated controls. They identified an extremely strong dominant association between rare variants in RNU4-2 and intellectual disability (posterior probability of association about 1; log Bayes factor 55). None of the 34 cases carrying the 3 top variants had previously received a diagnosis, and these cases were phenotypically more homogeneous than expected by chance. Greene et al. (2024) found 8 rare variants that were present only in affected participants. The variants lay in 2 contiguous regions of RNU4-2 (n.62-70 and n.73-79), within a locus markedly depleted of variation in gnomAD. Of the variants in 47 cases, 37 were de novo and 10 had unknown inheritance. Seven variants lay in the quasi-pseudoknot region: n.63T-G, n.64_65insG, n.64_65insT, n.65A-G, n.65_66insT, n.67A-G, and n.68_69insA. Two variants lay in stem III: n.76C-T and n.77_78insT. The most common variant, n.64_65insT, arose de novo in 33 different families. In 1 pedigree, the n.65A>G variant was found in a heterozygous male proband. His mother was called homozygous for the reference allele, but inspection of the aligned WGS reads suggested that she was likely mosaic for the variant.

paragraphs.text: In 115 individuals with NDD, Chen et al. (2024) identified heterozygous variants in RNU4-2, all located within an 18-bp region. In the Genomics England 100,000 Genomes Project, they found a highly recurrent single-base insertion, n.64_65insT (GRCh38 chr12:120291839:T:TA). It arose de novo in 38 probands sequenced with both unaffected parents, and findings in 8 more individuals were consistent with de novo occurrence. All 46 individuals had undiagnosed NDD, representing 0.52% of 8,841 undiagnosed NDD probands. The variant was absent from 3,408 diagnosed NDD probands, 21,817 non-NDD probands, 33,122 unaffected individuals, gnomAD v4.0, and All of Us. It was seen in only 1 individual in UK Biobank. Across all cohorts, 89 of the 115 affected individuals (77.4%) carried this variant. A second recurrent single-base insertion, n.77_78insT (GRCh38 chr12:120291826:T:TA), was found in 6 individuals, including 2 affected sibs. Other single-base insertions included n.68_69insA and n.64_65insG. In total, 100 individuals carried 6 different single-base insertions in the critical region. Single-base insertions in this region were present in 54 of 8,841 undiagnosed GEL NDD probands, compared with 2 of 490,132 UK Biobank individuals (odds ratio 1,531).

paragraphs.text: Greene et al. (2024) reported that one variant region of RNU4-2 maps to the U4-U6 quasi-pseudoknot interaction and the other maps to U4-U6 stem III. They predicted that the variants destabilize interactions of U4 snRNA with U6 snRNA and with RNA-binding proteins. They noted that G64 of U4 snRNA is thought to help stabilize the ACAGAGA loop of U6 snRNA, and they proposed that the n.64_65insT insertion could disrupt the G64(U4)-A47(U6) interaction that supports the quasi-pseudoknot. Because WBP4 deficiency causes a similar phenotype, they suggested that delayed U4-U6 unwinding may be the underlying mechanism of disease.

paragraphs.text: Chen et al. (2024) noted that the 18-bp critical region (nucleotides 62-79) is loaded into the active site of the BRR2 (SNRNP200) helicase. The n.64_65insT variant lies within a T-loop (quasi-pseudoknot), and n.77_78insT lies in the stem III region that pairs with U6. The authors proposed that single-base insertions destabilize the U4/U6 interaction and/or alter the positioning of the U6 ACAGAGA sequence that receives the 5-prime splice site. They analyzed blood RNA-seq data from 5 individuals with RNU4-2 variants: 3 with n.64_65insT, 1 with n.77_78insT, and 1 with n.78A-C. Compared with controls, these individuals had significantly more abnormal splicing events at unannotated 5-prime splice sites (mean 8.8 vs 0.7). Splicing events shared by 2 or more patients were not found in any of 378 controls. At sites with increased use, positions +3 to +5, which pair with the U6 ACAGAGA sequence, had shifted away from the consensus. The authors concluded that the variants disrupt accurate recognition of 5-prime splice sites during spliceosome activation.
